title: Ontario Has a Math Emergency
author: Nidhi Sachdeva
summary: Nidhi Sachdeva exposes Ontario's Grade 6 mathematics crisis as an instructional problem stemming from pedagogical choices, not an ability problem among students. Only half of students meet provincial standards, affecting 134,000 students with real consequences for science, trades, and financial literacy. Low student confidence at just 39% stems directly from discovery-based teaching lacking explicit instruction. Cognitive science demonstrates that students need clear explanation, modeling, and guided practice before reasoning about new concepts, yet current approaches reverse this evidence-based sequence. The Matthew Effect compounds inequality: students with tutoring accelerate while others disengage, widening equity gaps. High-performing education systems like Singapore, Japan, and Estonia have long built their math programs on explicit instruction with foundational fluency before problem-solving.
points: Only 50% of Ontario Grade 6 students meet math standards, affecting 134,000 students with real consequences for science, trades, and financial literacy.
Student confidence in math has collapsed to 39%, with hesitation preventing persistence and intellectual risk-taking even among capable learners.
Inquiry-first teaching without explicit instruction violates what cognitive science shows about working memory limitations and knowledge retention.
The Matthew Effect compounds inequality: students with tutoring accelerate while others disengage, widening equity gaps even as standardized teaching improves.
Alignment with how learning actually works requires explicit instruction, guided practice, and foundational fluency to enable problem-solving and reasoning.
quotes: Students cannot reason effectively about ideas they have not yet learned. Working memory is limited. Without clear explanations, modelling and guided practice, even capable learners become overwhelmed.
Knowledge frees up thinking. Fluency makes problem-solving possible. Crucially, explicit instruction benefits the students who struggle the most.

We would never hand a child a flute and ask them to discover how to play before teaching notes and scales. Nor would we start swim lessons in the deep end. Yet in math, we often reverse this sequence.

Countries with high-performing education systems, such as Singapore, Japan and Estonia, have long built their math programs on these principles. Britain has recently moved in the same direction, with measurable gains.

If Ontario wants better outcomes, three actions are clearly needed: strengthen teacher education in evidence-based math instruction; adopt curriculum materials that guide teachers toward clarity rather than guesswork; and build foundational fluency with math facts early and explicitly.” Archived from Science of Learning on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
